title: The Pawnshop Bandoneón: New York, Corrientes, the rue Ballu, and the Murder of the Tango
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Rivadavia 2527, Mar del Plata: the birth
stops.date_confidence: attested. La Capital de Mar del Plata gives the address and the hour, about two in the morning, with a midwife attending. The coordinates are a fresh geocode of the street number; an earlier estimate in the research pool sat about 1.1 km southwest of the actual site and is not used here.
stops.campa: In a two-storey house on Rivadavia, a few blocks in from the sea, Asunta Manetti is delivered of a son at about two in the morning, a midwife attending. He is the only child Vicente Piazzolla will have, and they name him Astor after a friend of his father's, the violinist Astor Bolognini. Everyone calls Vicente by another name, Nonino, and that name will outlive the man who carried it by a wide margin. Mar del Plata in 1921 is a resort town of Italian immigrants and empty winters. A commercial gallery stands on the site now, with two plaques on it.
suggested_refs: The plaques at Rivadavia 2527, Mar del Plata, on the site of the birth house
Municipio de General Pueyrredón, official biography page
sources: Diario La Capital de Mar del Plata, 'La promesa de Astor y Nonino'
Diario La Capital de Mar del Plata, 'Todo empezó en una casa de dos plantas ubicada en la calle Rivadavia'

stops.name: Lower East Side, Manhattan: the family lands
stops.date_confidence: contested year. English Wikipedia gives 1925 for the emigration; Spanish Wikipedia gives 1924. The month is nowhere recorded and defaults to January. No building address was found; the pin marks the neighbourhood.
stops.campa: The Piazzollas cross the Atlantic and take rooms in the immigrant quarter of lower Manhattan, where Vicente works as a barber. The boy grows up on English and on whatever comes through the windows. A childhood illness has left him with a limp and he is small for his age, so he fights often. Argentina is a country his parents talk about at the table, in a language he answers in with an accent. Tango reaches him the way everything else in that flat reaches him, secondhand: his father's phonograph, running in the evenings after the shop has closed.
suggested_refs: The Lower East Side tenement blocks of the mid-1920s Argentine and Italian emigration

stops.name: Lower East Side, Manhattan: the pawnshop bandoneón
stops.date_confidence: contested. English Wikipedia and the Wise Music Classical composer page give 1929; Spanish Wikipedia gives 1927 and adds a price of eighteen dollars. Neither the year nor the price is settled, and the month is unrecorded.
stops.campa: Vicente comes home from a pawnshop with a secondhand bandoneón, an instrument built in Germany for churches too poor to buy organs and taken up instead by the tango orchestras of Buenos Aires. He wants his son to play the music of the country they left. Astor wants to play whatever the boys on the block are playing. He is eight, and he learns it anyway: on the floor of the apartment, the box worked open and shut against his knees, the straps still too long for his arms.
suggested_refs: The German bandoneón trade and its adoption by the Buenos Aires orquesta típica
sources: Wise Music Classical, composer page for Astor Piazzolla

stops.name: Little Italy, Manhattan: back from the Depression
stops.date_confidence: attested for the sequence, approximate for the month. Argentine sources have the crash sending the family back to Mar del Plata at the beginning of 1930 and returning them to New York at the beginning of 1931, when the Little Italy move occurs. An earlier dating of 1930 for this resettlement is a year early.
stops.campa: The crash sends the family back to Mar del Plata at the start of 1930, and a year of that is enough: they return to New York at the beginning of 1931 and settle this time in Little Italy. Vicente cuts hair. Astor is ten, bilingual, an Argentine among Italians, and he carries the bandoneón to whatever will have it. The blocks between Mulberry and Mott sit close enough to the water that he can hear the ships working at night, and the tenement windows stay open through the summer.
suggested_refs: The 1930-31 Depression-era round trip between New York and Mar del Plata
sources: acercandonoscultura.com.ar, on the Piazzolla family's New York years

stops.name: Lower Manhattan: Béla Wilda's open window
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year and the teacher; the address of Wilda's studio is not given in any source consulted, so the pin is neighbourhood-level. Piazzolla told the story himself in a 1976 interview reprinted by Todotango.
stops.campa: Passing a building in the neighbourhood, the boy hears a piano being worked at for nine hours a day and stops in the street to listen. The pianist is Béla Wilda, Hungarian, a former pupil of Rachmaninoff, and he agrees to take the boy on. Wilda puts Bach in front of him and has him transcribe the fugues for bandoneón, which is not what the instrument was built to do. The counterpoint that later gets him called a murderer of the tango is learned here, in a room he found by ear from the pavement, from a teacher whose address no source records. He is twelve.
suggested_refs: Todotango.com, 'Piazzolla: his childhood in New York', reprint of a 1976 interview
sources: Todotango.com, 'Piazzolla: his childhood in New York'
Wise Music Classical, composer page for Astor Piazzolla

stops.name: 310 East 44th Street, Manhattan: the errand to Gardel
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1934 and for the Beaux-Arts Apartments, where the Fundación Carlos Gardel places Gardel from January 1934 in an eighteenth-floor penthouse. One variant account says 48th Street rather than 44th, and an earlier pin in the research pool sat 1.6 km away in Times Square. The film is released in 1935, which is why some timelines date the meeting to that year.
stops.campa: Vicente carves a small wooden gaucho and sends his son across town with it to the Beaux-Arts Apartments, where Carlos Gardel has taken a penthouse on the eighteenth floor. The pianist Alberto Castellano opens the door. Gardel keeps the carving, keeps the boy, and puts him to work: at thirteen he plays a paper boy in El día que me quieras and interprets for the singer around New York. Gardel invites him along on the tour that ends the following June in a burning aeroplane at Medellín. Vicente refuses to let him go.
suggested_refs: El día que me quieras (Paramount, 1935), the newsboy scene
The Beaux-Arts Apartments, 307-310 East 44th Street, Gardel's New York residence from January 1934
sources: La Nación, 'El mágico encuentro entre Piazzolla y Gardel en Nueva York'
Diario Norte, 'Cuando Piazzolla conoció a Gardel'

stops.name: Alberti 1561, Mar del Plata: the return
stops.date_confidence: the return to Argentina in 1936 is attested by English Wikipedia; the street address rests on a single Mar del Plata newspaper and has not been cross-checked against a second source. Coordinates are a fresh geocode of that address. Month unrecorded.
stops.campa: The family comes home for good and takes a house on Alberti, inland from the beach. Astor is fifteen and speaks Spanish with an American accent. He keeps at the bandoneón in a town that empties every autumn, playing where a bandoneón is wanted, which in Mar del Plata out of season means weddings and cafés. Two years later he leaves for Buenos Aires with the instrument and nothing arranged at the other end. The address for the house on Alberti rests on one local newspaper and no more.
suggested_refs: Diario La Capital de Mar del Plata, 'La promesa de Astor y Nonino'
sources: Diario La Capital de Mar del Plata, 'La promesa de Astor y Nonino'

stops.name: Avenida Corrientes, Buenos Aires: seventeen and looking for work
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1938; no month and no first venue is named in any source, so this sits on the canonical Buenos Aires pin used across the atlas rather than at an address.
stops.campa: He arrives at seventeen in the only city on earth where his instrument is the national one. Corrientes runs from the docks to the theatres and does not close; the cabarets along it hire bandoneonists the way other trades hire hands. He works for Francisco Lauro, then for Gabriel Clausi, learning the repertoire from inside the fila, the row of bandoneóns that sits at the front of an orquesta típica and breathes together. No source names a first venue. The street itself is the whole of the address.
suggested_refs: The Avenida Corrientes cabaret strip of the late 1930s, hiring ground of the orquestas típicas

stops.name: Buenos Aires: the chair in Troilo's orchestra
stops.date_confidence: Spanish Wikipedia dates the debut to December 1939 and English Wikipedia agrees on the year; some general-audience accounts, including the dossier this file was built against, put it in 1938. The more specific December 1939 dating is followed and the conflict is left standing.
stops.campa: Aníbal Troilo, the finest bandoneonist in the country and a bandleader at twenty-four, takes him on as a substitute and then keeps him. Piazzolla is eighteen. He plays in the fila and begins writing arrangements, and the arrangements are the trouble: he keeps putting things into them that dancers cannot dance to, and Troilo keeps striking those things out with a blue pencil. The apprenticeship runs five years and the argument inside it never settles. Piazzolla will say for the rest of his life that Troilo taught him everything he knows.
suggested_refs: The Orquesta Típica Aníbal Troilo, 1939-1944, and Piazzolla's arrangements for it

stops.name: Buenos Aires: the lessons with Ginastera
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1941-1946 by English Wikipedia and by Caras y Caretas, 'Los maestros de Astor'; the Wise Music Classical page starts them in 1940. No address for the lessons has been found, so this uses the canonical Buenos Aires pin. The chain of introduction is often given as Rubinstein alone; Juan José Castro is the intervening link.
stops.campa: Arthur Rubinstein, passing through Buenos Aires in 1940, hears the young bandoneonist's concerto and sends him to Juan José Castro; Castro declines to teach him and passes him on to Alberto Ginastera. Piazzolla becomes Ginastera's first private pupil and stays six years, going in the mornings with scores and coming out with orchestration, harmony, and the habit of writing for instruments he does not play. At night he works the cabarets, and the two educations do not meet for another decade. The lessons run to 1946. No source names the room they happened in.
suggested_refs: Fundación Juan March, 'Piazzolla, alumno de Ginastera'
Caras y Caretas, 'Los maestros de Astor', 5 March 2021
sources: Caras y Caretas, 'Los maestros de Astor'
Fundación Juan March, 'Piazzolla, alumno de Ginastera'

stops.name: Buenos Aires: the marriage to Dedé Wolff
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction as to precision, attested as to fact. Interlude, 'Tango Passion: Astor Piazzolla and Dedé Wolff', gives a civil ceremony at the end of October 1942 with a church ceremony two days later; Spanish Wikipedia agrees on October 1942; English Wikipedia's timeline gives 1943 and is the single dissenting source. No church or registry is named, so this sits on the canonical Buenos Aires pin.
stops.campa: He marries Odette Wolff, called Dedé, a painter he met at a tea party; the civil ceremony falls at the end of October and the church follows two days after. Diana is born the next year and Daniel the year after that. Dedé paints. Astor plays until four in the morning and writes in the hours after that. It is a household of two working artists in a city where that is not a living, and it is organised throughout around his hours rather than hers. The marriage lasts twenty-four years.
suggested_refs: Diana Piazzolla, Astor (Buenos Aires, 1987), the daughter's memoir of the household
sources: Interlude, 'Tango Passion: Astor Piazzolla and Dedé Wolff'

stops.name: Buenos Aires: out of Troilo's orchestra
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1944 for the departure and the Fiorentino ensemble, and for 1946 for the founding of his own orquesta típica and the Odeón recordings. Months unrecorded.
stops.campa: He leaves Troilo and takes the singer Francisco Fiorentino with him, forming his own ensemble; two years later he builds an orquesta típica under his own name and records steadily for Odeón. Fiorentino sings, the floors fill, the payroll is met. It is also, by his own reckoning afterwards, a dance orchestra playing what dance orchestras play, while the music he actually wants is being written at home in the small hours. The blue pencil is gone and he discovers that he has brought the argument with him.
suggested_refs: The Odeón recordings of the Orquesta Típica Astor Piazzolla, 1946-1949

stops.name: Buenos Aires: the orchestra disbanded
stops.date_confidence: contested year. English Wikipedia gives 1950; the dossier this file was built against gives 1949. Sources are not unanimous and the month is unrecorded.
stops.campa: He breaks up the orchestra. There is no other work to go to and there are two children at home, so he takes arranging jobs and film scores and spends the rest of the hours on symphonic writing nobody has commissioned. Sources put the disbanding at 1949 or at 1950. What is not in dispute is the shape of the decision: a man holding the national instrument stops playing it professionally in order to write for strings and winds. It costs him most of four years of income. What he told Dedé, or whether he asked her at all, is not in anything consulted here.
suggested_refs: Piazzolla's Argentine film scores of the early 1950s, written during the years without an orchestra

segments.name: The Fistfight Symphony and the Rue Ballu

stops.name: Facultad de Derecho, Buenos Aires: Sevitzky, two bandoneóns, trompadas
stops.date_confidence: attested for 16 August 1953 by La Nación, 'Astor Piazzolla: noche de sinfonía, bandoneones y trompadas', and historiadelasinfonia.es. The work itself was composed in 1951, which is what some sources are dating when they give that year. The research pool's earlier claim that the contest was judged in the United States is wrong: Sevitzky conducted the premiere in Buenos Aires himself.
stops.campa: Buenos Aires (Tres movimientos sinfónicos), written two years earlier, takes the prize in the competition judged by Fabien Sevitzky, and Sevitzky himself conducts the premiere in the auditorium of the law faculty at the head of the Radio del Estado symphony orchestra. Piazzolla has scored two bandoneóns into the orchestra. A part of the audience takes this as an insult offered to both traditions at once, and the evening ends in fistfights among the cultured. The prize carries a French government scholarship with it.
stops.quote: I was writing symphonies, chamber music, string quartets.
stops.quote_source: Astor Piazzolla, interviewed by Tony Staveacre, quoted at maramarietta.com
suggested_refs: Buenos Aires (Tres movimientos sinfónicos), 1951, scored for orchestra with two bandoneóns
sources: La Nación, 'Astor Piazzolla: noche de sinfonía, bandoneones y trompadas'

stops.name: 36 rue Ballu, Paris: what instrument do you play, then
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1954 and for the French government scholarship; the month is not recorded and defaults to January. The dialogue is reconstruction: four incompatible wordings of Boulanger's verdict circulate, one of them naming the tango Triunfal and giving no quotation at all. The wording carried here is the question, which the Gorin memoir transmits and which the retellings do not contradict.
stops.campa: He climbs to Nadia Boulanger's apartment with a folder of symphonies and chamber music and nothing of the tango in it. She reads the scores and finds them well made and dead, Stravinsky here, Bartók there, Ravel there, and no Piazzolla anywhere in them. He is thirty-three and has spent months not telling this woman what he does for a living. Then she asks. He confesses the cabarets, the bandoneón, the tango, and she makes him play one at the piano. A few bars in, she stops him and takes his hands.
stops.quote: You say that you are not pianist. What instrument do you play, then?
stops.quote_source: Attributed to Nadia Boulanger in Piazzolla's own recollection, Natalio Gorin, Astor Piazzolla: A Memoir, trans. Fernando González (Amadeus Press, 2001), as reproduced at thelistenersclub.com, 'Astor Piazzolla at 100' (2021)
suggested_refs: Nadia Boulanger's apartment at 36 rue Ballu, Paris, and her Wednesday class
Piazzolla's Paris year, 1954-1955, on a French government scholarship
sources: Wise Music Classical, composer page for Astor Piazzolla
maramarietta.com, 'Piazzolla, Astor: Tango Zero Hour', Tony Staveacre interview

stops.name: Paris: the tango called Nonino
stops.date_confidence: attested that a tango titled Nonino was written in Paris in 1954, per the English Wikipedia article on Adiós Nonino; the month is unknown and is placed late in the scholarship year only to order the segment. The Fontainebleau strand of the Boulanger studies, which some sources place at the Conservatoire Américain rather than the rue Ballu apartment, is not resolved by anything consulted.
stops.campa: Between lessons he writes a tango and calls it Nonino, after his father. It is one of several pieces the Paris year turns out and it makes no particular mark. Five years from now, in an apartment in New York with his father three days dead, he will open it again, keep its lyrical section, and build around it the piece that is played at his own funeral. In 1954 it is simply a tango named for a barber from Mar del Plata. The same scholarship also buys him conducting lessons under Hermann Scherchen.
stops.quote: I threw away ten years' work and started with my New Tango in 1954.
stops.quote_source: Astor Piazzolla, interviewed by Tony Staveacre, quoted at maramarietta.com
suggested_refs: Nonino (Paris, 1954), the tango later reworked as Adiós Nonino
The Conservatoire Américain at Fontainebleau, the unresolved second location of the Boulanger studies

stops.name: Buenos Aires: the Octeto Buenos Aires
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1955 by English Wikipedia; no founding venue is named anywhere, so this sits on the canonical Buenos Aires pin. The ensemble dissolves in 1958.
stops.campa: Home with Boulanger's verdict, he puts eight players together: two bandoneóns, two violins, cello, double bass, piano, and an electric guitar, which no tango orchestra has ever carried. There is no singer and there is nowhere to dance. What he has built is a chamber ensemble that happens to be playing tango. He is thirty-four, and this is the group in which nuevo tango starts, in a city that within a year will have found another name for it. The Octeto lasts three years and records for Allegro before it comes apart.
stops.quote: For me, tango was always for the ear rather than the feet.
stops.quote_source: Astor Piazzolla, quoted at thelistenersclub.com, 'Astor Piazzolla at 100' (2021); the interview of origin is not named on the page
suggested_refs: The Octeto Buenos Aires, 1955-1958, and its recordings for Allegro
sources: El País (English edition), 'Astor Piazzolla: Argentina celebrates tango killer turned national treasure'

stops.name: Buenos Aires: the name they give him
stops.date_confidence: tradition. The label asesino del tango is widely reported across the retrospective press, but the best-known illustration of it, the taxi driver who recognises him and puts him out of the cab, traces to his widow Laura Escalada's recollection in later journalism and to no dated first-hand account. The date is placed in 1955 only to order the segment.
stops.campa: The traditionalists name him asesino del tango, the tango assassin, and the name holds for thirty years. Radio stations drop him. Musicians will not sit in. The story told most often, from his widow's recollection rather than from any dated record, is of a taxi driver who recognises the face, refuses the fare, and puts him out on the pavement for having killed the tango. Nothing dates that scene. He keeps the name and starts using it himself, opening interviews with it.
stops.quote: They call me the Tango Assassin.
stops.quote_source: Astor Piazzolla, quoted at pleasekillme.com, 'Astor Piazzolla, The Tango Assassin at 100'; the article says he often began interviews this way but names no specific interview
suggested_refs: El País (English edition), 'Astor Piazzolla: Argentina celebrates tango killer turned national treasure'
sources: pleasekillme.com, 'Astor Piazzolla, The Tango Assassin at 100'
El País (English edition), on the tango-killer label

stops.name: Facultad de Derecho, Buenos Aires: the two acetates
stops.date_confidence: contested year, unrecorded month. The Instituto Nacional de Musicología 'Carlos Vega' dates this concert to 1956; the chronology assembled for this file also carries an entry dating the same event to 1957 and calling it the ensemble's first public performance. No source consulted calls it a debut, and the month is not given, so an earlier '1956-10' would assert precision nothing supports.
stops.campa: The Octeto plays the auditorium of the law faculty, the same hall where the fistfights broke out three years earlier, and this time the concert is one of the group's rare outright successes. Someone cuts two acetates that night. They disappear for sixty-five years, surface in 2021 in the hands of a collector, Ezequiel Lodeiro, and are digitised: the only surviving live recording of the Octeto, and the only recording of Tango Ballet, the one work Piazzolla wrote expressly for the eight.
stops.quote: My musicians were threatened, but I was the troublemaker. People there just can't take it, somebody changing the music they used to love forty or fifty years ago.
stops.quote_source: Astor Piazzolla, quoted at pleasekillme.com, 'Astor Piazzolla, The Tango Assassin at 100'; the originating interview is not named on the page
suggested_refs: Instituto Nacional de Musicología 'Carlos Vega', 'El Octeto Buenos Aires de Astor Piazzolla', the digitised 1956 acetates
Tango Ballet, the only work written expressly for the Octeto
sources: Instituto Nacional de Musicología 'Carlos Vega', 'El Octeto Buenos Aires de Astor Piazzolla'

stops.name: East 92nd Street, New York: the arranger's years
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1958 for the relocation and for the family's presence; the East 92nd Street address is attested only for 1959, when Adiós Nonino was written there, and is used for this stop as the nearest documented residence. Month unrecorded.
stops.campa: He gives up on Buenos Aires and moves the family to New York, where nobody has heard of the tango assassin because nobody has heard of him. He arranges for other people, writes a jazz-tango that satisfies neither party, and takes what work appears. Almost nothing from these two years is music he was willing to defend afterwards. The apartment is on East 92nd Street, and Dedé and the children are in it with him. The address is documented for 1959 only.
suggested_refs: Piazzolla's 1958-1960 New York arranging work and the jazz-tango experiments of those years
sources: Infobae, 'El dolor que llevó a Astor Piazzolla a componer Adiós Nonino' (20 June 2021)

stops.name: San Juan, Puerto Rico: the Club Flamboyán and the news
stops.date_confidence: attested for October 1959 and for the Club Flamboyán engagement, per the English Wikipedia article on Adiós Nonino and Infobae's 2021 account. No source gives the club's address, so the pin is city-level. The research pool separately carried a 1960 Club Flamboyán stop; that is the same engagement, misdated.
stops.campa: He is working an engagement at the Club Flamboyán in San Juan, on tour with the dancers Juan Carlos Copes and María Nieves, when word comes from Mar del Plata that Vicente is dead. He does not go to the funeral. He finishes what he can, flies back to New York, and shuts himself in the apartment; Dedé takes the children out and leaves him alone in it. He is thirty-eight, and the man who put the instrument in his hands is gone. No source consulted gives the address of the club.
suggested_refs: The Compañía Argentina Tangolandia tour of Puerto Rico, autumn 1959
sources: Infobae, 'El dolor que llevó a Astor Piazzolla a componer Adiós Nonino'

stops.name: East 92nd Street, New York: forty-five minutes
stops.date_confidence: attested that the piece was written in the New York apartment on East 92nd Street a few days after the October 1959 death, in about forty-five minutes, reworking the lyrical section of the 1954 Paris tango Nonino. The exact day is not recorded and is placed mid-month to order the segment. Spanish Wikipedia's timeline dates the composition to 1962, which contradicts the death date the same source gives.
stops.campa: Alone in the apartment a few days after the news, he takes out Nonino, the tango he wrote in Paris five years earlier, keeps its lyrical section, and builds something else around it. Dedé has taken the children out; the door stays shut. It takes about forty-five minutes. Adiós Nonino becomes the piece he plays at the end of every concert for the rest of his life, in every hall, on four continents, for thirty-one years. He said afterwards that he never wrote anything better and could not account for where it came from.
suggested_refs: Adiós Nonino (1959), inducted into the Latin Grammy Hall of Fame in 2001
sources: Infobae, 'El dolor que llevó a Astor Piazzolla a componer Adiós Nonino'

stops.name: Buenos Aires: the first Quinteto Nuevo Tango
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1960 by both English and Spanish Wikipedia; month unrecorded, no founding venue named, canonical Buenos Aires pin.
stops.campa: Back in Buenos Aires he cuts the ensemble down to five: bandoneón, violin, piano, electric guitar, double bass. It is the smallest group that can carry everything he wants and the loudest way available of saying that the dance orchestra is finished. Five men, no singer, no floor. He has been a working musician for twenty-two years by now. In one line-up or another, the quintet is the group he keeps coming back to for the next thirty, and nearly all the music that made his name is written for it.
suggested_refs: The first Quinteto Nuevo Tango, 1960, and its recordings for the label Antar and others

stops.name: Philharmonic Hall, Lincoln Center, New York: the quintet on a subscription stage
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1965 by Strings Magazine, 'Tango Titan'; the month is not given. The concert is often misattributed to Carnegie Hall, and that conflation is corrected rather than repeated here.
stops.campa: The quintet plays Philharmonic Hall at Lincoln Center and the concert is issued as a record. This is the city where he learned English and carried a pawnshop bandoneón up to a Hungarian pianist's door; he comes back to it as a bandleader on a subscription stage, with a programme of his own music and nothing borrowed in it. New York is easier to him than Buenos Aires and will stay that way to the end. The same year he writes Verano Porteño for a play. The other three seasons are still four years off, and nothing at this point says there will be others.
suggested_refs: Strings Magazine, 'Tango Titan: Remembering Composer and Bandoneon Master Astor Piazzolla at 100'

stops.name: Buenos Aires: the contract with Horacio Ferrer
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1967 and for a five-year exclusivity agreement. The often-repeated figure of over two hundred songs is off by roughly an order of magnitude: Ferrer's own collection, Quereme así piantao: Los tangos de Piazzolla y Ferrer (1967-1971), gathers about twenty-eight. Month unrecorded.
stops.campa: He signs a five-year exclusive agreement with the poet Horacio Ferrer, who writes in lunfardo and a porteño surrealism and does not write like a tango lyricist. Piazzolla has never tied himself to one writer before. The partnership produces on the order of two dozen songs, not the two hundred often repeated. It is Ferrer's words that finally carry him to an audience standing outside the argument altogether. The traditionalists dislike the language as much as they dislike the harmony.
suggested_refs: Horacio Ferrer, Quereme así piantao: Los tangos de Piazzolla y Ferrer (1967-1971)
sources: Horacio Ferrer, Quereme así piantao (collected songs of the partnership)

stops.name: Sala Planeta, Suipacha 927, Buenos Aires: María de Buenos Aires
stops.date_confidence: attested for 8 May 1968 and for a run of roughly a hundred performances into the first week of September, per La Nación's fiftieth-anniversary piece. The venue address, Galería de las Américas, Suipacha 927, was located and geocoded for this file; the research pool had marked it as not found.
stops.campa: María de Buenos Aires opens at the Sala Planeta, in a gallery on Suipacha, on the eighth of May: an operita about a girl born in the slums who becomes the city, dies, and comes back as her own shadow. Amelita Baltar sings María. Ferrer's libretto is closer in shape to a mass than to a musical, and Piazzolla scores it for eleven players and a narrator. No tango stage has carried an operita before. It runs about a hundred performances, into the first week of September.
suggested_refs: María de Buenos Aires (1968), libretto by Horacio Ferrer, first recording with Amelita Baltar
sources: La Nación, 'María de Buenos Aires, la operita de Piazzolla y Ferrer, cumple medio siglo'

stops.name: Buenos Aires: Balada para un loco
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1969 in substance through English Wikipedia's account of the Ferrer years; Spanish Wikipedia's timeline dates the composition to 1964, three years before the Ferrer contract that the same timeline lists for 1967, which is an internal inconsistency in that source and is not resolved here. Month unrecorded.
stops.campa: Ferrer's lyric puts a madman on Callao at six in the evening, telling a woman that he is flying. Piazzolla sets it. The record then sells in numbers no tango of his has come near, and for the first time the man they call the assassin of the tango has a hit; the people buying it were never in the argument to begin with. Amelita Baltar sings it at a festival in Buenos Aires, and half the hall boos her while the other half applauds. Spanish Wikipedia dates the song to 1964, three years before the Ferrer contract its own timeline gives.
suggested_refs: Balada para un loco (1969), lyrics by Horacio Ferrer, sung by Amelita Baltar

stops.name: Teatro Regina, Buenos Aires: the four seasons together
stops.date_confidence: attested for 19 May 1970 as the premiere of the complete set, per English Wikipedia's own timeline. Coordinates are a fresh geocode of Avenida Santa Fe 1235; the research pool's earlier pin sat about a kilometre away. The claim that the cycle was composed in 1965 is wrong: only Verano Porteño dates from 1965.
stops.campa: On the nineteenth of May the four seasons of Buenos Aires are played together for the first time, at the Teatro Regina on Santa Fe. Verano came in 1965, written for a play; Otoño, Invierno and Primavera follow across 1969 and 1970, composed as separate pieces and made into a set only afterwards. They are not a cycle in the Vivaldi sense and Piazzolla did not plan them as one. No source consulted says who decided to play the four together, or when the decision was taken. Concert halls have programmed them alongside Vivaldi's ever since.
suggested_refs: Las cuatro estaciones porteñas, composed 1965-1970, premiered complete 19 May 1970
sources: Teatro Regina, Avenida Santa Fe 1235, Buenos Aires

stops.name: Teatro Colón, Buenos Aires: with Troilo, bandoneóns in hand
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. The single piece of evidence located is a Wikimedia Commons photograph captioned as Piazzolla with Aníbal Troilo at the Teatro Colón in 1972; the full provenance of the image was not verified beyond the Commons metadata, and no month is given. The nonet Conjunto 9 is dated to September 1971 by Wise Music Classical and to 1970 by English Wikipedia, unresolved.
stops.campa: He appears at the Colón with Aníbal Troilo, the bandleader whose blue pencil struck out his arrangements thirty-three years before, the two of them sitting with bandoneóns on the grandest stage in the country. The house that stands for official Argentine music receives the man accused of murdering the national one, and receives him alongside its guardian. He is fifty-one and has spent seventeen years being told he is not a man of tango. The evidence for the occasion is one photograph and its caption.
stops.quote: I still can't believe that some pseudo-critics continue to accuse me of having murdered tango. They have it backward. They should look at me as the saviour of tango. I performed plastic surgery on it.
stops.quote_source: Astor Piazzolla, quoted in The Arts Desk, 'Interview: Quinteto Astor Piazzolla on playing in London and why Mick Jagger's a fan'; the paper attributes it only with 'once declared' and names no originating interview
suggested_refs: Wikimedia Commons, 'Astor Piazzolla with Aníbal Troilo, Teatro Colón 1972'
Conjunto 9 (Conjunto Nueve), founded 1970 or September 1971

stops.name: Rome: the heart, and the offer from Pagani
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1973 for the heart attack and the move to Italy; no month, no residential address, city-level pin.
stops.campa: His heart fails him. Argentina is coming apart at the same time, and when the publisher Aldo Pagani makes him an offer he takes it and moves to Italy, where most of the next five years will be spent. The exile is commercial as much as political: European studios, European money, and audiences with no stake whatever in the question of whether the tango has been murdered. He records more in these five years than in any other stretch of his life. He is fifty-two.
suggested_refs: The Aldo Pagani management years, 1973-1978, and the Italian recordings

stops.name: Milan: Libertango, and Summit with Mulligan
stops.date_confidence: attested for May 1974 for the Libertango sessions in Milan and September 1974 for Summit; the specific studio is not named in any source consulted, so the pin is city-level and the two sessions may or may not share a room. Both are folded into one stop for that reason.
stops.campa: In a Milan studio in May he records Libertango: eight bars of ostinato under a bandoneón that never quite lands where the beat is. It becomes the most covered thing he ever wrote and the one piece of his that people who have never heard his name can hum. In September, in Italy again, he records Summit with the baritone saxophonist Gerry Mulligan, nuevo tango and American jazz put in one room to see what happens. Neither session is documented down to the studio.
suggested_refs: Libertango (Carosello, 1974)
Summit (Reunión Cumbre), with Gerry Mulligan, 1974

stops.name: Buenos Aires: the dinner with Videla
stops.date_confidence: attested in substance for 1976 through Piazzolla's own memoir account as quoted by Perfil, 'Astor Piazzolla en 100 datos', and through the surrounding Radiolandia and Gente interviews discussed at cabezademoog.blogspot.com. No exact date was located. The earlier framing of this as a gala at which he happened to be seated near Videla understates what the record shows.
stops.campa: Two men in black bring an envelope to his door with a letter saying the President is expecting him. He goes, and dines with Jorge Rafael Videla in the first year of a dictatorship that is disappearing people. In interviews around it he calls the musicians he has been recruiting egomaniacs, drug addicts and leftists. In 1976 that is not an opinion but a denunciation with consequences; Martín Graziano notes it came close to a death sentence. Julio Cortázar breaks off the friendship. His daughter Diana says she never forgave him.
stops.quote: They sent two men in black with an envelope and a letter saying President Videla was expecting me.
stops.quote_source: Astor Piazzolla's own memoir account, quoted in Perfil, 'Astor Piazzolla en 100 datos'
suggested_refs: Piazzolla's 1976-77 interviews in Radiolandia and Gente
Martín Graziano's account of the musicians' denunciation and its risk

stops.name: Buenos Aires: the Second Quintet
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1978 by English Wikipedia and the Wise Music Classical page; month unrecorded, canonical Buenos Aires pin. The quoted judgement concerns Tango: Zero Hour, recorded by this same ensemble in 1986.
stops.campa: He rebuilds the quintet with Pablo Ziegler at the piano and tours it for eleven years, the longest-running and best-documented ensemble of his life. The instrumentation is exactly that of 1960: bandoneón, violin, piano, electric guitar, bass. What has changed is that the halls are full and mostly abroad. He is fifty-seven and playing better than he has ever played. This group records Tango: Zero Hour in New York in 1986, and of everything he made he rated that one highest.
stops.quote: The greatest record I've made in my life. We gave our souls to it.
stops.quote_source: Astor Piazzolla on Tango: Zero Hour (1986), quoted in Fernando González's liner notes, reproduced at maramarietta.com
suggested_refs: Tango: Zero Hour (American Clavé, 1986), recorded by the Second Quintet

stops.name: Paris: the César for Tangos, el exilio de Gardel
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1986 for the award by English Wikipedia, the Wise Music Classical awards list, and the dossier; the exact ceremony date was not verified for this file and February is used to order the segment.
stops.campa: Fernando Solanas makes a film about Argentines waiting out the dictatorship in Paris, people who cannot go home, and Piazzolla writes the score: the bandoneón and the string figures that had been his own argument for thirty years, put to the use of other people's exile. The picture is named for Gardel, whose door he was sent to with a wooden gaucho at thirteen. Paris has been handing him verdicts since Boulanger read his symphonies in 1954, and this one arrives as a statuette: the French academy gives the film the César for best music. The date of the ceremony is not recorded in anything consulted here.
suggested_refs: Tangos, el exilio de Gardel (1985), dir. Fernando Solanas, score by Astor Piazzolla

stops.name: Montreux: the festival with Gary Burton
stops.date_confidence: attested for July 1986 by English Wikipedia; the exact day and the stage used that year are not confirmed, and the pin marks the festival grounds.
stops.campa: He plays the Montreux Jazz Festival with the vibraphonist Gary Burton, one more room in which the question of whether this is really tango does not come up, because nobody in it grew up with the tango. The jazz world took him in decades before Buenos Aires did. Switzerland, Germany, Italy, Japan, the United States: the itinerary of his last decade reads largely as a list of places that are not Argentina. He is sixty-five and touring more or less continuously.
stops.quote: In Argentina you could change hundreds of presidents, you could change religions, but you can't change the tango.
stops.quote_source: Astor Piazzolla, quoted at pleasekillme.com, 'Astor Piazzolla, The Tango Assassin at 100'; originating interview not named on the page
suggested_refs: The Montreux Jazz Festival appearance with Gary Burton, July 1986, later issued on record

stops.name: Central Park, New York: the open air
stops.date_confidence: attested for 6 September 1987 by English Wikipedia; the exact stage within the park is not confirmed and the pin marks central Central Park. The recording is released in 1994, after his death.
stops.campa: He plays in the open air in Central Park on a September evening, with the Second Quintet at the height of its eleven years, in the city where he learned to play at all. Sixty-two years earlier the family had come off a boat and taken rooms downtown. He plays Adiós Nonino at the end, as he does everywhere. Nothing in any account of the concert makes a ceremony of the return; he plays the programme and goes. The tape is issued seven years later as The Central Park Concert.
suggested_refs: The Central Park Concert (released 1994), recorded 6 September 1987

stops.name: Nakano Sun Plaza Hall, Tokyo: touring with Milva
stops.date_confidence: attested for 26 June 1988 by English Wikipedia.
stops.campa: He tours Japan with the Italian singer Milva and plays the Nakano Sun Plaza on the twenty-sixth of June. He is sixty-seven, his heart has already failed him once, and he is keeping a schedule that would be heavy for a man of forty. Japanese and European broadcasters keep tape rolling on a musician whom Argentine radio spent thirty years refusing to play. Tokyo has taken to the bandoneón as thoroughly as any city outside Buenos Aires, and the halls fill for a repertoire the audience cannot follow a word of.
suggested_refs: The 1988 Japanese tour with Milva, recorded for broadcast

stops.name: Buenos Aires: four bypasses, and a second marriage
stops.date_confidence: both events are dated 1988 by English Wikipedia without months; October is used to place the surgery after the June Tokyo concert, as the sources imply. The marriage date is contested: secondary accounts put the start of the partnership with Laura Escalada at 1976, and no source consulted reconciles that with a 1988 wedding.
stops.campa: Surgeons open his chest and give him four bypasses. In the same year he divorces Dedé Wolff and marries the singer Laura Escalada, whom secondary accounts have him with since the middle of the previous decade; how those two datings fit together, no source explains. He has been warned by everyone whose business it is to warn him. He is back on the road within months of the surgery, and in the twelve months after it he plays Amsterdam, London and New York.
suggested_refs: Laura Escalada Piazzolla and the Fundación Astor Piazzolla, custodians of the estate

stops.name: Koninklijk Theater Carré, Amsterdam: the bill with Pugliese
stops.date_confidence: attested that the two ensembles shared a bill at the Carré in June 1989; English Wikipedia gives 26 June in its Piazzolla article and 29 June in its Pugliese article, and Osvaldo Pugliese's own file in this atlas preserves the same discrepancy unresolved.
stops.campa: In a nineteenth-century circus theatre on the Amstel, his sextet shares a bill with the orchestra of Osvaldo Pugliese. Pugliese was accused in his own generation of ruining the tango by slowing it into something nobody could dance to; Piazzolla was accused of the same crime for the opposite reasons. Both men are old, both are condemned, both are on the same Dutch stage in the same week, and the house is full for them. The sources give two different dates for it.
suggested_refs: Koninklijk Theater Carré, Amstel 115-125, Amsterdam

stops.name: Power Station, New York: Five Tango Sensations
stops.date_confidence: attested for November 1989 for the sessions and for the Power Station, New York, as the room where the record was made and mixed, per Discogs credits and the Kronos Quartet's own account. Nonesuch releases it on 25 January 1991. The research pool's country-level placing of this session in the United States is narrowed here to the studio.
stops.campa: At the Power Station on West 53rd Street he records Five Tango Sensations with the Kronos Quartet: bandoneón and string quartet, written for them. The string quartet is the form Boulanger's pupils were supposed to write in, and he arrives at it at sixty-eight, with the instrument from the pawnshop across his knees. It is the last studio record he makes. Nonesuch releases it in January 1991, by which time he has been unable to speak for five months.
suggested_refs: Five Tango Sensations (Nonesuch, 1991), with the Kronos Quartet, recorded at Power Station, New York

stops.name: Athens: the last concert
stops.date_confidence: attested for 3 July 1990 by English Wikipedia; the hall is not named and the pin is city-level.
stops.campa: He plays with the Orchestra of Colours in Athens on the third of July, his own music, orchestrated. He is sixty-nine, and he has been working since the Corrientes cabarets took him on at seventeen, which is fifty-two years of nights. Nothing in any account of the evening suggests that anyone in the building, the players, the audience, or the composer, understood that this was the last one. Neither the hall nor the size of the orchestra is named in the sources. A month later he is in Paris.
suggested_refs: The Orchestra of Colours, Athens, 3 July 1990, Piazzolla's final concert

stops.name: Notre-Dame de Paris: the hemorrhage in the street
stops.date_confidence: contested, and the two versions cannot both stand. English Wikipedia gives 4 August 1990; the accounts that describe him walking to Sunday mass require 5 August, since 4 August 1990 was a Saturday. The Sunday framing is followed here and the conflict is recorded rather than smoothed. Coordinates for Notre-Dame are accurate.
stops.campa: On his way to Sunday mass at Notre-Dame with Laura Escalada, he suffers a cerebral hemorrhage in the street. He had come to Paris to prepare a performance and had been working the week before. He does not recover consciousness in any full sense again, and he never plays again. He is sixty-nine. Sources give the fourth of August and the fifth; the fourth was a Saturday, so either the date or the Sunday mass is wrong, and nothing consulted settles which.
suggested_refs: La Nación, 'Astor Piazzolla, un buen guía para anclar en París'
sources: La Nación, 'Astor Piazzolla, un buen guía para anclar en París'

stops.name: Hôpital Ambroise Paré, Boulogne-Billancourt: the diagnosis
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction as to the hospital. The name and the diagnosis reached this file through a Spanish-language search summary rather than a page read directly, and that caveat stands; the coordinates are a fresh geocode of 9 Avenue Charles de Gaulle. The day is placed immediately after the hemorrhage to order the segment.
stops.campa: He is taken to the hospital at Boulogne-Billancourt, just outside the western edge of Paris on the Seine, where the doctors find the brain damage irreversible. Laura Escalada arranges the flight home. He had written music at a keyboard every morning of his adult life, and he leaves France unable to write at all. The hospital's name reaches this account through a search summary rather than a document, and is set down with that caveat attached. The day he was admitted is not recorded anywhere.
suggested_refs: Hôpital Ambroise Paré, 9 Avenue Charles de Gaulle, Boulogne-Billancourt

stops.name: Palermo, Buenos Aires: twenty-three months
stops.date_confidence: the date and city are firmly attested by both English and Spanish Wikipedia. The clinic, given as a sanatorium in the Palermo neighbourhood, comes from a Spanish-language search summary that was not verified against a fetched primary source, so the pin is a neighbourhood placement rather than an address.
stops.campa: He lives twenty-three more months in Buenos Aires, in and out of coma, and dies on the fourth of July 1992, at seventy-one. The clinic is named in Spanish-language summaries as a sanatorium in Palermo; only the city and the date are firmly attested. Adiós Nonino, written in about forty-five minutes in a New York apartment thirty-three years earlier, is played over him. The country that spent thirty years calling him the assassin of its national music gives the death, at first, a modest notice.
suggested_refs: Konex de Honor, awarded posthumously to his family in 1995 as most important deceased Argentine musician of the decade
sources: Spanish-language biographical summary, aggregated via search

stops.name: Cementerio Jardín de Paz, Pablo Nogués: Sector 4, Manzana 3, Parcela 16
stops.date_confidence: attested for the cemetery and for the grave reference by Perfil and Find a Grave; the exact burial day is not recorded and is placed two days after the death. Ingeniero Pablo Nogués lies in the Partido de Malvinas Argentinas, not Pilar, and the Spanish Wikipedia category naming Pilar refers to a different site of the same cemetery chain. Coordinates are a fresh geocode.
stops.campa: He is buried not in Chacarita among the tango dead but in a garden cemetery at Ingeniero Pablo Nogués, in the partido of Malvinas Argentinas, at Sector 4, Manzana 3, Parcela 16. Mar del Plata has since put a bronze of him on the rambla and given his name to the airport, and a crater on Mercury carries the name too. The grave itself is a marble plaque set flush with the grass. There is no bandoneón carved on it, no portrait, no title of any piece. A journalist who went looking for it reported that the cemetery staff did not know whose grave it was.
